result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_regular()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph is regular (all nodes have the same degree). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L18271-L18358){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_regular() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is regular](/assets/graphs/is-regular.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a six-node cycle; the badges show every node has degree 2, so is_regular() returns True. Right: the same cycle plus a chord between C and F (shown in the accent color), which raises C and F to degree 3 while the rest stay at 2, so is_regular() returns False." width="100%"} A graph is regular if every node has the same degree. For directed graphs, this means all nodes have the same in-degree and the same out-degree (though in-degree and out-degree don't need to equal each other). Degrees are computed from all edges: parallel edges each count, and in an undirected graph a self-loop adds `2` to its node's degree (in a directed graph it adds `1` to both the in-degree and out-degree). Isolated nodes have degree `0`, so a single isolated node makes an otherwise regular graph irregular. Use `is_k_regular()` when you need a specific degree rather than just a uniform one. Regularity is a useful structural check when: - verifying that a generated lattice, ring, or other synthetic network is as uniform as intended - checking the assumptions of results that only hold for regular graphs (e.g. certain spectral bounds) - confirming that degree-based centrality can't distinguish any nodes (every node gets the same score in a regular graph) The whole graph is checked and the current selection is ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph is regular, `False` otherwise. Graphs with zero or one node are regular. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Empty graphs and single-node graphs pass vacuously, cycles are $2$-regular, and the complete graph $K_n$ is $(n - 1)$-regular. For directed graphs, both in-degree and out-degree must be constant across nodes, though the constants themselves don't need to agree, so a $k$-in-$\ell$-out schema is still regular. Regularity is the hypothesis behind many spectral shortcuts: the adjacency eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ equals the shared degree, and expander bounds like Cheeger's inequality assume it. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node in a cycle has exactly two neighbors, so cycles are always regular: ::: {#8964e584 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(5) graph.is_regular() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: A star's hub connects to every other node while each spoke connects only to the hub, so their degrees differ and the graph isn't regular: ::: {#13a4f9a9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_star_graph(4) graph.is_regular() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: In a complete graph, every node connects to all `n - 1` others, so all degrees match: ::: {#f5a1d4d5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_full_graph(n=5) graph.is_regular() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: In a directed cycle every node has one incoming and one outgoing edge, so it is regular. A directed path is not: its first node has no incoming edge and its last node no outgoing edge: ::: {#af6f7fda .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed_cycle = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_cycle_graph(n=4) directed_path = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_path_graph(n=4) directed_cycle.is_regular(), directed_path.is_regular() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
